name: Squill Blue
lede: Squill Blue is a light, airy blue named for the squill flower and first fixed by Robert Ridgway's 1912 systematic color atlas.

sections.title: Ridgway's plate XX, by way of a flower
sections.body:
Ridgway's 1912 *Color Standards and Color Nomenclature* places this hue on plate XX, hue 45 prime, tone b, and the ISCC-NBS circular of 1955 cites the same block, classing it a light blue [1]. Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary records the same name, also dated to 1912, confirming Ridgway as the earliest source among the systems our library tracks [1]. The books read do not explain the name beyond the plant it is presumably drawn from, the blue-flowered squill, and that link is undocumented here as a stated fact rather than an inference [1].

The nearest named colors on file are [[iceberg]], [[aero]] and [[blue-jeans]], at 3.3, 3.4 and 4.2 ΔE [1]. It also sits near [[cornflower]] in our library, a slightly more saturated relative [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color within six units of Squill Blue covers at least one per cent of the canvas in 48 paintings, about 0.2 per cent overall, rarer than 59 per cent of the named colors we track; the within-painting lens finds it in 25 [2]. It peaks in the 1900s, in 5 of 1,674 paintings, present in 0.3 per cent of the 1,674 paintings (5 of them) we hold from that century, 2.2 times the archive's overall rate [2]. Inside a painting it most often sits as a mid-tone, in 36 per cent of its 25 appearances [2].

It is over-represented in France, 11 of 3,443 paintings, 2.5 times expected [2]. The earliest dated painting to carry it is from 1482, by Piero di Cosimo, 430 years before Ridgway's own 1912 record, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [2]. In printed English the phrase *squill blue* peaks in the 1930s and rose fastest in the 1920s, by Google Books' count of every sense of the words [3]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, read as screen colors, not pigment identifications[2].
